title: Japan Sees Rise in Southeast Asian Residents
paragraphs: The number of foreign residents in Japan has reached a new record, and people from Southeast Asian countries are making up a growing share of them.

According to Japan's Immigration Services Agency, there were about 4.28 million foreign residents in Japan at the end of June 2026, not including short-term visitors. That was an increase of about 156,000 from the end of 2025, and it means that foreign residents now make up roughly 3.5% of Japan's population.

Many of the newcomers are from Southeast Asia. Vietnam had the second-largest group of foreign residents in Japan, with 693,750 people, while the Philippines had 362,761. Some of the fastest growth came from Myanmar and Indonesia. Among the ten largest groups, the number of residents from Myanmar rose by 15.9%, and the number from Indonesia rose by 15.6%.

Work is one of the main reasons for this growth. Japan's population is shrinking quickly, and many industries are struggling to find enough workers. To deal with this problem, Japan created the "specified skilled worker" visa program, which allows foreign workers to fill jobs in fields such as nursing care, construction and food production. By the end of June, a record 444,256 foreign residents were in Japan under this program. Workers from Vietnam formed the largest group, while Indonesia and Myanmar also sent large numbers.

Toshihiro Menju, an expert on immigration, said that with Japan's population falling by more than 900,000 a year, the country has no choice but to rely on foreign workers. Menju expects the number of foreign residents to reach 10 million in the 2040s.

However, immigration has become a sensitive political issue in Japan. The government recently made it harder to get permanent residency, requiring higher incomes and better Japanese language skills. Menju warned that if permanent residency becomes too difficult to obtain, fewer people may want to stay in Japan for the long term.
